questions.question: Describe da Gama's voyage from Lisbon to the east coast of southern Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Da Gama left Lisbon in July 1497 with four ships and roughly one hundred and seventy men. He sailed in a great curve far out into the Atlantic, out of sight of land for about three months, and reached St Helena Bay in November 1497, where a meeting with the Khoikhoi ended in a fight. At Mossel Bay, the meeting began peacefully with music, dancing and trade, but the Khoikhoi later knocked down the padrão. On Christmas Day 1497, he named the coast Natal.

questions.question: Explain how da Gama reached India and why his voyage was important.
questions.expected_answer: At Malindi, the friendly ruler gave him an experienced pilot who knew the monsoon winds, and the ships crossed the Indian Ocean to Calicut in May 1498. It was the first European voyage from Europe to India by sea. Although many sailors died of scurvy and only two ships returned, the spices were worth many times the cost, and Portugal controlled the sea route to the East for about a hundred years.

questions.question: Why did the VOC set up a station at the Cape, and how did it affect the Khoikhoi?
questions.expected_answer: VOC ships needed fresh food and water on the long voyage to Asia to fight scurvy, and the Haarlem shipwreck crew showed that vegetables could grow at the Cape. In 1652, Jan van Riebeeck set up a refreshment station with a fort and a vegetable garden and traded with the Khoikhoi for cattle. From 1657, farms along the Liesbeek River took Khoikhoi grazing land and water, war broke out in 1659, and over time the Khoikhoi lost much of their land and cattle.
